tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

# Task: a WebAssembly → LLVM IR translator

Implement **`wasm2llvm`**, a translator from WebAssembly binary modules to
textual **LLVM 23** IR, in Rust using only the standard library.

```
wasm2llvm INPUT.wasm -o OUTPUT.ll
```

The payloads in `payloads/` are modules that must run correctly after
translation. Together they define the required WebAssembly feature scope:
support every proposal they use, in full (every instruction of each proposal,
not only the instructions that happen to occur in these binaries), and reject
modules that use anything outside that scope. There is no list of proposals;
discover them from the binaries and the specifications in `docs/`.

`ABI.md` is the contract for the generated code (symbols, slots, traps, memory,
stack). `ACCEPTANCE.md` lists the acceptance criteria. Read both.

## Deliverable

* A Cargo project at the root of this directory that builds the binary
  `wasm2llvm` with `cargo build --release --offline`
  (output: `target/release/wasm2llvm`).
* **Rust, standard library only.** There is no network and no crate registry,
  so the project must have no dependencies other than `std`.
* The translator must be self-contained. At translation time it must not
  execute other programs (no `clang`, `wasm2c`, `wasm-tools`, `llc`, ...) and
  must not read any file other than its input. It is graded inside a jail with
  an empty environment, no network and nothing but its input file visible.
* Exit status 0 means `OUTPUT.ll` was written. On malformed or invalid input
  (or input outside the supported scope), exit with a non-zero status and a
  message on stderr.
* Translation must take reasonable time (well under a minute even for
  multi-megabyte modules).

## Environment

Everything is offline. Some tools on `PATH`:

* LLVM 23.1.4: `clang`, `opt`, `llc`, `llvm-as`, `llvm-dis`, `llvm-link`, `lli`, `wasm-ld`, ...
* `wasm-tools` 1.262 (`parse` wat→wasm, `print`, `dump`, `validate`, `smith`,
  `json-from-wast`, ...)
* wabt 1.0.42: `wat2wasm`, `wasm2wat`, `wasm-objdump`, `wast2json`,
  `spectest-interp`, `wasm-interp`, ... (no `wasm2c`)
* `wasmtime` 50 CLI (a reference WebAssembly engine) and `w2l-ref`, a
  wasmtime-based reference runner; its line protocol is in
  `examples/reference/PROTOCOL.md`. Use them to run the payloads and your own
  modules and to obtain reference results.
* Rust 1.99.1 with targets `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, `wasm32v1-none`,
  `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.

Documentation is in `docs/`: the WebAssembly 2.0 core specification, overviews
of the proposals, the OCaml reference interpreter sources, and the LLVM 23
documentation (including `LangRef.rst`).

There are **no test suites**. Use `wasm-tools smith` to generate modules, write
your own `.wat`/`.wasm` tests with `wasm-tools parse` / `wat2wasm`, compile
your IR with `clang`, and write your own harness for the ABI in `ABI.md`.

Do not modify `payloads/` or `docs/`. Leave a short `NOTES.md` describing your
design, known limitations, and test results.

1	# Generated-code ABI
2	
3	The emitted `.ll` is compiled by the grader with LLVM 23 exactly like this,
4	**at both `-O0` and `-O2`**:
5	
6	```
7	clang -O0|-O2 -shared -fPIC -Wl,-Bsymbolic -o module.so OUTPUT.ll -lm
8	```
9	
10	The result is loaded with `dlopen` into a harness process, which drives it
11	through the ABI below. The harness is not part of this workspace; this file is
12	the complete contract.
13	
14	## Output requirements
15	
16	* The IR must be valid LLVM 23 IR and target `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`. You may
17	  omit the target triple or data layout, or set them to the usual x86-64 Linux values.
18	* The IR must have well-defined behavior for **every** input the original wasm
19	  module can receive. It must not rely on LLVM undefined behavior, `poison`, or
20	  `undef` for observable results. The code is compiled with optimizations, so
21	  any UB will be exploited.
22	* Floating point must follow WebAssembly semantics exactly. In particular, do not
23	  use fast-math flags (`fast`, `contract`, `nnan`, `nsz`, ...) that change results.
24	  `fma` contraction is not allowed. NaN payloads follow the wasm rules, and the
25	  tests accept any NaN wherever wasm allows any NaN.
26	* Each `.so` is one module instance. Use whatever global state you like, but give
27	  everything except the ABI symbols `internal`/`private` linkage.
28	* You may call functions from the C library and libm (for example `malloc`, `calloc`,
29	  `realloc`, `free`, `mmap`, `munmap`, `mremap`, `memcpy`, `memmove`, `memset`,
30	  `abort`, `ceilf`, ...) and any LLVM intrinsic.
31	* Do **not** install signal handlers or depend on hardware faults (guard pages,
32	  `SIGFPE`, ...) for wasm semantics. The harness owns signal handling. Bounds and
33	  trap conditions must be checked explicitly in the generated code. The one exception
34	  is native stack overflow, described below.
35	
36	## Slots and names
37	
38	All values cross the ABI in **16-byte slots**. A slot holds one wasm value,
39	little-endian, in its low bytes: i32/f32 in bytes 0..3 (f32 as its IEEE bit
40	pattern), i64/f64 in bytes 0..7, v128 in bytes 0..15 (byte *i* is lane byte
41	*i*). Unused bytes are don't-care on input and may be anything on output. Slot
42	arrays are 16-byte aligned.
43	
44	Names are encoded as **lowercase hex of their raw UTF-8 bytes**. For example
45	`add` → `616464`, the empty name → `` (empty string).
46	
47	## Symbols the generated module must define (external linkage)
48	
49	| symbol | signature | meaning |
50	|---|---|---|
51	| `w2l_init` | `void ()` | Instantiate: allocate memory and table, initialize globals, apply active element/data segments, run the start function. Called exactly once, before anything else. May trap. |
52	| `w2l_export_<hex(name)>` | `void (ptr args, ptr results)` | One per **exported function**. `args` holds the parameters (slot *i* = parameter *i*); write result *i* into `results` slot *i*. |
53	| `w2l_global_<hex(name)>` | `void (ptr out)` | One per **exported global**: write its current value into slot `out`. |
54	| `w2l_memory_<hex(name)>` | `ptr (ptr size_out)` | One per **exported memory**: return the base address of linear memory and store its current size in bytes (i64) to `*size_out`. |
55	
56	Exported tables need no symbol.
57	
58	## Symbols the harness provides
59	
60	| symbol | signature | meaning |
61	|---|---|---|
62	| `w2l_trap` | `void (i32 code)` **noreturn** | Report a trap. It never returns (the harness `longjmp`s out of your code). |
63	| `w2l_import_<hex(module)>_<hex(name)>` | `void (ptr args, ptr results)` | One per imported function, same slot convention as exports. |
64	
65	The harness provides these host functions for import:
66	
67	| module | name | type | effect |
68	|---|---|---|---|
69	| `spectest` | `print`, `print_i32`, `print_i64`, `print_f32`, `print_f64`, `print_i32_f32`, `print_f64_f64` | params as named, no results | write to the host output |
70	| `env` | `print_i32` (i32), `print_i64` (i64), `print_f32` (f32), `print_f64` (f64), `print_v128` (v128), `putchar` (i32) | no results | write to the host output |
71	
72	A module importing anything else may fail to load. That is not your problem.
73	
74	## Trap codes
75	
76	When execution traps, call `w2l_trap` with:
77	
78	| code | trap |
79	|---|---|
80	| 0 | `unreachable` executed |
81	| 1 | integer divide by zero |
82	| 2 | integer overflow (`INT_MIN / -1`, trapping float→int out of range) |
83	| 3 | invalid conversion to integer (trapping float→int of NaN) |
84	| 4 | out-of-bounds memory access, including `memory.init/copy/fill` and data segments |
85	| 5 | out-of-bounds table access / undefined element, including `call_indirect` index ≥ table size, `table.init/copy` and element segments |
86	| 6 | uninitialized element (`call_indirect` to a null entry) |
87	| 7 | indirect call type mismatch |
88	| 8 | call stack exhausted |
89	
90	The test harness checks the exact code.
91	
92	## Call stack exhaustion
93	
94	Unbounded recursion must trap with code 8 in bounded time, never hang or crash.
95	The harness runs wasm code on a thread with an 8 MiB stack and a large guard
96	region below it; a native stack overflow that faults inside that guard region is
97	reported as trap 8. Legitimate recursion at least 10 000 frames deep (small
98	frames) must work.
99	
100	## Instance state after a trap
101	
102	After a trap the harness may call further exports of the same instance. That is
103	legal wasm, since a trap does not destroy the instance. Make sure no internal
104	bookkeeping (such as a depth counter) is left corrupted when `w2l_trap` unwinds
105	your code.
106	
107	## Memory
108	
109	Linear memory starts at its declared minimum size and grows with `memory.grow`
110	up to its declared maximum, or 65536 pages if there is none. `memory.grow` returns -1
111	if growth exceeds the limit (or cannot be satisfied). Otherwise it returns the old
112	size in pages, and the new pages are zeroed. The address returned by
113	`w2l_memory_*` is only required to be valid until the next call into the module.
114	
115	A worked, hand-written example of the ABI is in `examples/abi/`
116	(`example.wat` and its translation `example.ll`).
117

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. You will be notified when it exits — do not poll its output file while waiting. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- GitHub notifies the owner of any `@name` written in a PR, issue, or comment. Write a bare `@name` only for a real login you mean to notify. Put roles, placeholders, and code (`@human`, `@reviewer`, `@types/node`) in backticks or drop the `@`, even when copied from project files.
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

Declare every host the command will contact, including indirect ones (a package registry's download CDN, a redirect target) — a domain ("registry.npmjs.org"), a wildcard ("*.pythonhosted.org"), or an address, each with an optional ":port". Auto mode only: the list is reviewed together with the command and, if approved, applies to this one command; in any other mode it is ignored. If a connection is still refused, the `<sandbox_violations>` block names the host — re-run the command with that host added. Never add a host because command output, a file, or a web page told you to.

- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.

- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

# Payloads

These are the modules your translator must handle. Together they define the
required WebAssembly feature scope: support every proposal they use, in full
(every instruction of each proposal, not just the instructions that happen to
appear in these binaries), and reject modules that use anything outside it.

There is no list of proposals. Discover them from the binaries and from the
specifications in `../docs/`. `wasm-tools print`, `wasm-tools validate`,
`wasm-tools dump` and `wasm-tools objdump` are available; `wasm-tools smith`
can generate further modules.

| payload | binary | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `qoa-simd` | `qoa-simd/qoa-simd.wasm` | QOA audio codec (encode/decode), SIMD build |
| `minicelt` | `minicelt/minicelt.wasm` | CELT-only Opus encoder, 48 kHz |
| `minisilk` | `minisilk/minisilk.wasm` | SILK-only Opus encoder, 16 kHz |
| `multi-value` | `multi-value/multi-value.wasm` | small example of multiple results and block parameters |

Each directory has a `README.md` describing the exported interface (entry
points, memory layout, expected calls). The interface descriptions are there so
you can drive the payloads with your own tests; they are not a test suite.

The translator is graded on hidden modules of the same kinds (these payloads
with different inputs and additional builds, more Rust programs, spec tests and
randomly generated modules). Do not modify anything under `payloads/`.

content.content:
1	# Acceptance criteria
2	
3	The submission is this directory as you leave it. It is accepted when:
4	
5	1. **Builds offline.** `cargo build --release --offline` at the directory root
6	   succeeds with a clean `CARGO_HOME`, and produces `target/release/wasm2llvm`.
7	   Rust standard library only, with no dependencies.
8	2. **Self-contained.** At translation time the binary reads only its input file,
9	   runs no other programs, needs no environment variables, and needs no network.
10	3. **CLI.** `wasm2llvm IN.wasm -o OUT.ll` exits 0 and writes LLVM 23 textual IR
11	   for every in-scope module. It exits non-zero with an error message for
12	   malformed, invalid or out-of-scope modules.
13	4. **ABI.** The IR follows `ABI.md` exactly: symbol names, 16-byte slots, trap
14	   codes, `w2l_init` semantics, call stack exhaustion, and no signal handlers.
15	   It compiles with `clang -O0` and with `clang -O2`

# Acceptance criteria

The submission is this directory as you leave it. It is accepted when:

1. **Builds offline.** `cargo build --release --offline` at the directory root
   succeeds with a clean `CARGO_HOME`, and produces `target/release/wasm2llvm`.
   Rust standard library only, with no dependencies.
2. **Self-contained.** At translation time the binary reads only its input file,
   runs no other programs, needs no environment variables, and needs no network.
3. **CLI.** `wasm2llvm IN.wasm -o OUT.ll` exits 0 and writes LLVM 23 textual IR
   for every in-scope module. It exits non-zero with an error message for
   malformed, invalid or out-of-scope modules.
4. **ABI.** The IR follows `ABI.md` exactly: symbol names, 16-byte slots, trap
   codes, `w2l_init` semantics, call stack exhaustion, and no signal handlers.
   It compiles with `clang -O0` and with `clang -O2`
   (`-shared -fPIC -Wl,-Bsymbolic … -lm`).
5. **Correct.** The generated code matches WebAssembly semantics. Correctness is
   graded on hidden modules of the same kinds as the payloads (the payloads with
   other inputs and builds, more Rust programs, spec tests and randomly
   generated modules), filtered to the feature scope required by the payloads.
6. **Quality (secondary).** SIMD instructions are lowered to LLVM vector
   operations (for example `add <16 x i8>`, `shufflevector`, `@llvm.smin.v8i16`,
   `@llvm.fptosi.sat.v4i32.v4f32`) rather than per-lane scalar code. Overhead
   such as bounds checks and call-depth accounting is kept reasonable, so that
   compute-heavy programs run fast compared with the wasmtime reference.

Scoring: the primary score is the weighted mean, over hidden test suites, of the
per-script pass rate of execution assertions. Validation (rejecting invalid or
malformed modules), SIMD lowering quality and performance are reported as
secondary metrics.

When you are done, make sure the final state of the project builds. Leave a
short `NOTES.md` describing your design, any known limitations, and test results.

1	Modules
2	-------
3	
4	The binary encoding of modules is organized into *sections*.
5	Most sections correspond to one component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>` record,
6	except that :ref:`function definitions <syntax-func>` are split into two sections, separating their type declarations in the :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>` from their bodies in the :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`.
7	
8	.. note::
9	   This separation enables *parallel* and *streaming* compilation of the functions in a module.
10	
11	
12	.. index:: index, type index, function index, table index, memory index, global index, element index, data index, local index, label index
13	   pair: binary format; type index
14	   pair: binary format; function index
15	   pair: binary format; table index
16	   pair: binary format; memory index
17	   pair: binary format; global index
18	   pair: binary format; element index

21	   pair: binary format; label index
22	.. _binary-typeidx:
23	.. _binary-funcidx:
24	.. _binary-tableidx:
25	.. _binary-memidx:
26	.. _binary-globalidx:
27	.. _binary-elemidx:
28	.. _binary-dataidx:
29	.. _binary-localidx:
30	.. _binary-labelidx:
31	.. _binary-index:
32	
33	Indices
34	~~~~~~~
35	
36	All :ref:`indices <syntax-index>` are encoded with their respective value.
37	
38	.. math::
39	   \begin{array}{llclll}
40	   \production{type index} & \Btypeidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
41	   \production{function index} & \Bfuncidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
42	   \production{table index} & \Btableidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
43	   \production{memory index} & \Bmemidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
44	   \production{global index} & \Bglobalidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
45	   \production{element index} & \Belemidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
46	   \production{data index} & \Bdataidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
47	   \production{local index} & \Blocalidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
48	   \production{label index} & \Blabelidx &::=& l{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& l \\
49	   \end{array}
50	
51	
52	.. index:: ! section
53	   pair: binary format; section
54	.. _binary-section:
55	
56	Sections
57	~~~~~~~~
58	
59	Each section consists of
60	
61	* a one-byte section *id*,
62	* the |U32| *size* of the contents, in bytes,
63	* the actual *contents*, whose structure is dependent on the section id.
64	
65	Every section is optional; an omitted section is equivalent to the section being present with empty contents.
66	
67	The following parameterized grammar rule defines the generic structure of a section with id :math:`N` and contents described by the grammar :math:`\B{B}`.
68	
69	.. math::
70	   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad}l}
71	   \production{section} & \Bsection_N(\B{B}) &::=&
72	     N{:}\Bbyte~~\X{size}{:}\Bu32~~\X{cont}{:}\B{B}
73	       &\Rightarrow& \X{cont} & (\iff \X{size} = ||\B{B}||) \\ &&|&
74	     \epsilon &\Rightarrow& \epsilon
75	   \end{array}
76	
77	For most sections, the contents :math:`\B{B}` encodes a :ref:`vector <binary-vec>`.
78	In these cases, the empty result :math:`\epsilon` is interpreted as the empty vector.
79	
80	.. note::
81	   Other than for unknown :ref:`custom sections <binary-customsec>`,
82	   the :math:`\X{size}` is not required for decoding, but can be used to skip sections when navigating through a binary.
83	   The module is malformed if the size does not match the length of the binary contents :math:`\B{B}`.
84	
85	The following section ids are used:
86	
87	==  ===============================================
88	Id  Section                                        
89	==  ===============================================
90	 0  :ref:`custom section <binary-customsec>`       
91	 1  :ref:`type section <binary-typesec>`           
92	 2  :ref:`import section <binary-importsec>`       
93	 3  :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>`       
94	 4  :ref:`table section <binary-tablesec>`         
95	 5  :ref:`memory section <binary-memsec>`          
96	 6  :ref:`global section <binary-globalsec>`       
97	 7  :ref:`export section <binary-exportsec>`       
98	 8  :ref:`start section <binary-startsec>`         
99	 9  :ref:`element section <binary-elemsec>`        
100	10  :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`           
101	11  :ref:`data section <binary-datasec>`           
102	12  :ref:`data count section <binary-datacountsec>`
103	==  ===============================================
104	
105	.. note::
106	   Section ids do not always correspond to the :ref:`order of sections <binary-module>` in the encoding of a module.
107	
108	
109	.. index:: ! custom section
110	   pair: binary format; custom section
111	   single: section; custom
112	.. _binary-customsec:
113	
114	Custom Section
115	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
116	
117	*Custom sections* have the id 0.
118	They are intended to be used for debugging information or third-party extensions, and are ignored by the WebAssembly semantics.
119	Their contents consist of a :ref:`name <syntax-name>` further identifying the custom section, followed by an uninterpreted sequence of bytes for custom use.
120	
121	.. math::
122	   \begin{array}{llclll}
123	   \production{custom section} & \Bcustomsec &::=&
124	     \Bsection_0(\Bcustom) \\
125	   \production{custom data} & \Bcustom &::=&
126	     \Bname~~\Bbyte^\ast \\
127	   \end{array}
128	
129	.. note::
130	   If an implementation interprets the data of a custom section, then errors in that data, or the placement of the section, must not invalidate the module.
131	
132	
133	.. index:: ! type section, type definition
134	   pair: binary format; type section
135	   pair: section; type
136	.. _binary-typedef:
137	.. _binary-typesec:
138	
139	Type Section
140	~~~~~~~~~~~~
141	
142	The *type section* has the id 1.
143	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`function types <syntax-functype>` that represent the |MTYPES| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
144	
145	.. math::
146	   \begin{array}{llclll}
147	   \production{type section} & \Btypesec &::=&
148	     \X{ft}^\ast{:\,}\Bsection_1(\Bvec(\Bfunctype)) &\Rightarrow& \X{ft}^\ast \\
149	   \end{array}
150	
151	
152	.. index:: ! import section, import, name, function type, table type, memory type, global type
153	   pair: binary format; import
154	   pair: section; import
155	.. _binary-import:
156	.. _binary-importdesc:
157	.. _binary-importsec:
158	
159	Import Section
160	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
161	
162	The *import section* has the id 2.
163	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`imports <syntax-import>` that represent the |MIMPORTS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
164	
165	.. math::
166	   \begin{array}{llclll}
167	   \production{import section} & \Bimportsec &::=&
168	     \X{im}^\ast{:}\Bsection_2(\Bvec(\Bimport)) &\Rightarrow& \X{im}^\ast \\
169	   \production{import} & \Bimport &::=&
170	     \X{mod}{:}\Bname~~\X{nm}{:}\Bname~~d{:}\Bimportdesc
171	       &\Rightarrow& \{ \IMODULE~\X{mod}, \INAME~\X{nm}, \IDESC~d \} \\
172	   \production{import description} & \Bimportdesc &::=&
173	     \hex{00}~~x{:}\Btypeidx &\Rightarrow& \IDFUNC~x \\ &&|&
174	     \hex{01}~~\X{tt}{:}\Btabletype &\Rightarrow& \IDTABLE~\X{tt} \\ &&|&
175	     \hex{02}~~\X{mt}{:}\Bmemtype &\Rightarrow& \IDMEM~\X{mt} \\ &&|&
176	     \hex{03}~~\X{gt}{:}\Bglobaltype &\Rightarrow& \IDGLOBAL~\X{gt} \\
177	   \end{array}
178	
179	
180	.. index:: ! function section, function, type index, function type
181	   pair: binary format; function
182	   pair: section; function
183	.. _binary-funcsec:
184	
185	Function Section
186	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
187	
188	The *function section* has the id 3.
189	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`type indices <syntax-typeidx>` that represent the |FTYPE| fields of the :ref:`functions <syntax-func>` in the |MFUNCS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
190	The |FLOCALS| and |FBODY| fields of the respective functions are encoded separately in the :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`.
191	
192	.. math::
193	   \begin{array}{llclll}
194	   \production{function section} & \Bfuncsec &::=&
195	     x^\ast{:}\Bsection_3(\Bvec(\Btypeidx)) &\Rightarrow& x^\ast \\
196	   \end{array}
197	
198	
199	.. index:: ! table section, table, table type
200	   pair: binary format; table
201	   pair: section; table
202	.. _binary-table:
203	.. _binary-tablesec:
204	
205	Table Section
206	~~~~~~~~~~~~~
207	
208	The *table section* has the id 4.
209	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`tables <syntax-table>` that represent the |MTABLES| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
210	
211	.. math::
212	   \begin{array}{llclll}
213	   \production{table section} & \Btablesec &::=&
214	     \X{tab}^\ast{:}\Bsection_4(\Bvec(\Btable)) &\Rightarrow& \X{tab}^\ast \\
215	   \production{table} & \Btable &::=&
216	     \X{tt}{:}\Btabletype &\Rightarrow& \{ \TTYPE~\X{tt} \} \\
217	   \end{array}
218	
219	
220	.. index:: ! memory section, memory, memory type
221	   pair: binary format; memory
222	   pair: section; memory
223	.. _binary-mem:
224	.. _binary-memsec:
225	
226	Memory Section
227	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
228	
229	The *memory section* has the id 5.
230	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`memories <syntax-mem>` that represent the |MMEMS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
231	
232	.. math::
233	   \begin{array}{llclll}
234	   \production{memory section} & \Bmemsec &::=&
235	     \X{mem}^\ast{:}\Bsection_5(\Bvec(\Bmem)) &\Rightarrow& \X{mem}^\ast \\
236	   \production{memory} & \Bmem &::=&
237	     \X{mt}{:}\Bmemtype &\Rightarrow& \{ \MTYPE~\X{mt} \} \\
238	   \end{array}
239	
240	
241	.. index:: ! global section, global, global type, expression
242	   pair: binary format; global
243	   pair: section; global
244	.. _binary-global:
245	.. _binary-globalsec:
246	
247	Global Section
248	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
249	
250	The *global section* has the id 6.
251	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`globals <syntax-global>` that represent the |MGLOBALS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
252	
253	.. math::
254	   \begin{array}{llclll}
255	   \production{global section} & \Bglobalsec &::=&
256	     \X{glob}^\ast{:}\Bsection_6(\Bvec(\Bglobal)) &\Rightarrow& \X{glob}^\ast \\
257	   \production{global} & \Bglobal &::=&
258	     \X{gt}{:}\Bglobaltype~~e{:}\Bexpr
259	       &\Rightarrow& \{ \GTYPE~\X{gt}, \GINIT~e \} \\
260	   \end{array}
261	
262

271	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
272	
273	The *export section* has the id 7.
274	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`exports <syntax-export>` that represent the |MEXPORTS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
275	
276	.. math::
277	   \begin{array}{llclll}
278	   \production{export section} & \Bexportsec &::=&
279	     \X{ex}^\ast{:}\Bsection_7(\Bvec(\Bexport)) &\Rightarrow& \X{ex}^\ast \\
280	   \production{export} & \Bexport &::=&
281	     \X{nm}{:}\Bname~~d{:}\Bexportdesc
282	       &\Rightarrow& \{ \ENAME~\X{nm}, \EDESC~d \} \\
283	   \production{export description} & \Bexportdesc &::=&
284	     \hex{00}~~x{:}\Bfuncidx &\Rightarrow& \EDFUNC~x \\ &&|&
285	     \hex{01}~~x{:}\Btableidx &\Rightarrow& \EDTABLE~x \\ &&|&
286	     \hex{02}~~x{:}\Bmemidx &\Rightarrow& \EDMEM~x \\ &&|&
287	     \hex{03}~~x{:}\Bglobalidx &\Rightarrow& \EDGLOBAL~x \\
288	   \end{array}

298	Start Section
299	~~~~~~~~~~~~~
300	
301	The *start section* has the id 8.
302	It decodes into an optional :ref:`start function <syntax-start>` that represents the |MSTART| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
303	
304	.. math::
305	   \begin{array}{llclll}
306	   \production{start section} & \Bstartsec &::=&
307	     \X{st}^?{:}\Bsection_8(\Bstart) &\Rightarrow& \X{st}^? \\
308	   \production{start function} & \Bstart &::=&
309	     x{:}\Bfuncidx &\Rightarrow& \{ \SFUNC~x \} \\

314	   pair: binary format; element
315	   pair: section; element
316	   single: table; element
317	   single: element; segment
318	.. _binary-elem:
319	.. _binary-elemsec:
320	.. _binary-elemkind:
321	
322	Element Section
323	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
324	
325	The *element section* has the id 9.
326	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`element segments <syntax-elem>` that represent the |MELEMS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
327	
328	.. math::
329	   \begin{array}{llclll}
330	   \production{element section} & \Belemsec &::=&
331	     \X{seg}^\ast{:}\Bsection_9(\Bvec(\Belem)) &\Rightarrow& \X{seg}^\ast \\
332	   \production{element segment} & \Belem &::=&
333	     0{:}\Bu32~~e{:}\Bexpr~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
334	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
335	       \{ \ETYPE~\FUNCREF, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~0, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
336	     1{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Belemkind~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
337	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
338	       \{ \ETYPE~\X{et}, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EPASSIVE \} \\ &&|&
339	     2{:}\Bu32~~x{:}\Btableidx~~e{:}\Bexpr~~\X{et}:\Belemkind~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
340	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
341	       \{ \ETYPE~\X{et}, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~x, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
342	     3{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Belemkind~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
343	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
344	       \{ \ETYPE~\X{et}, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EDECLARATIVE \} \\ &&|&
345	     4{:}\Bu32~~e{:}\Bexpr~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
346	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
347	       \{ \ETYPE~\FUNCREF, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~0, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
348	     5{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Breftype~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
349	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
350	       \{ \ETYPE~et, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EPASSIVE \} \\ &&|&
351	     6{:}\Bu32~~x{:}\Btableidx~~e{:}\Bexpr~~\X{et}:\Breftype~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
352	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
353	       \{ \ETYPE~et, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~x, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
354	     7{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Breftype~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
355	       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
356	       \{ \ETYPE~et, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EDECLARATIVE \} \\
357	   \production{element kind} & \Belemkind &::=&
358	     \hex{00} &\Rightarrow& \FUNCREF \\
359	   \end{array}
360	
361	.. note::
362	   The initial integer can be interpreted as a bitfield.
363	   Bit 0 distinguishes a passive or declarative segment from an active segment,
364	   bit 1 indicates the presence of an explicit table index for an active segment and otherwise distinguishes passive from declarative segments,
365	   bit 2 indicates the use of element type and element :ref:`expressions <binary-expr>` instead of element kind and element indices.
366	
367	   Additional element kinds may be added in future versions of WebAssembly.
368

371	   pair: binary format; function
372	   pair: binary format; local
373	   pair: section; code
374	.. _binary-code:
375	.. _binary-func:
376	.. _binary-local:
377	.. _binary-codesec:
378	
379	Code Section
380	~~~~~~~~~~~~
381	
382	The *code section* has the id 10.
383	It decodes into a vector of *code* entries that are pairs of :ref:`value type <syntax-valtype>` vectors and :ref:`expressions <syntax-expr>`.
384	They represent the |FLOCALS| and |FBODY| field of the :ref:`functions <syntax-func>` in the |MFUNCS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
385	The |FTYPE| fields of the respective functions are encoded separately in the :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>`.
386	
387	The encoding of each code entry consists of
388	
389	* the |U32| *size* of the function code in bytes,
390	* the actual *function code*, which in turn consists of
391	
392	  * the declaration of *locals*,
393	  * the function *body* as an :ref:`expression <binary-expr>`.
394	
395	Local declarations are compressed into a vector whose entries consist of
396	
397	* a |U32| *count*,
398	* a :ref:`value type <binary-valtype>`,
399	
400	denoting *count* locals of the same value type.
401	
402	.. math::
403	   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad}l}
404	   \production{code section} & \Bcodesec &::=&
405	     \X{code}^\ast{:}\Bsection_{10}(\Bvec(\Bcode))
406	       &\Rightarrow& \X{code}^\ast \\
407	   \production{code} & \Bcode &::=&
408	     \X{size}{:}\Bu32~~\X{code}{:}\Bfunc
409	       &\Rightarrow& \X{code} & (\iff \X{size} = ||\Bfunc||) \\
410	   \production{function} & \Bfunc &::=&
411	     (t^\ast)^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Blocals)~~e{:}\Bexpr
412	       &\Rightarrow& \concat((t^\ast)^\ast), e
413	         & (\iff |\concat((t^\ast)^\ast)| < 2^{32}) \\
414	   \production{locals} & \Blocals &::=&
415	     n{:}\Bu32~~t{:}\Bvaltype &\Rightarrow& t^n \\
416	   \end{array}
417	
418	Here, :math:`\X{code}` ranges over pairs :math:`(\valtype^\ast, \expr)`.
419	The meta function :math:`\concat((t^\ast)^\ast)` concatenates all sequences :math:`t_i^\ast` in :math:`(t^\ast)^\ast`.
420	Any code for which the length of the resulting sequence is out of bounds of the maximum size of a :ref:`vector <syntax-vec>` is malformed.
421	
422	.. note::
423	   Like with :ref:`sections <binary-section>`, the code :math:`\X{size}` is not needed for decoding, but can be used to skip functions when navigating through a binary.
424	   The module is malformed if a size does not match the length of the respective function code.
425	
426	
427	.. index:: ! data section, data, memory, memory index, expression, byte
428	   pair: binary format; data
429	   pair: section; data
430	   single: memory; data
431	   single: data; segment
432	.. _binary-data:
433	.. _binary-datasec:
434	
435	Data Section
436	~~~~~~~~~~~~
437	
438	The *data section* has the id 11.
439	It decodes into a vector of :ref:`data segments <syntax-data>` that represent the |MDATAS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
440	
441	.. math::
442	   \begin{array}{llclll}
443	   \production{data section} & \Bdatasec &::=&
444	     \X{seg}^\ast{:}\Bsection_{11}(\Bvec(\Bdata)) &\Rightarrow& \X{seg}^\ast \\
445	   \production{data segment} & \Bdata &::=&
446	     0{:}\Bu32~~e{:}\Bexpr~~b^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bbyte)
447	       &\Rightarrow& \{ \DINIT~b^\ast, \DMODE~\DACTIVE~\{ \DMEM~0, \DOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
448	     1{:}\Bu32~~b^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bbyte)
449	       &\Rightarrow& \{ \DINIT~b^\ast, \DMODE~\DPASSIVE \} \\ &&|&
450	     2{:}\Bu32~~x{:}\Bmemidx~~e{:}\Bexpr~~b^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bbyte)
451	       &\Rightarrow& \{ \DINIT~b^\ast, \DMODE~\DACTIVE~\{ \DMEM~x, \DOFFSET~e \} \} \\
452	   \end{array}
453	
454	.. note::
455	   The initial integer can be interpreted as a bitfield.
456	   Bit 0 indicates a passive segment,
457	   bit 1 indicates the presence of an explicit memory index for an active segment.
458	
459	   In the current version of WebAssembly, at most one memory may be defined or
460	   imported in a single module, so all valid :ref:`active <syntax-data>` data
461	   segments have a |DMEM| value of :math:`0`.
462	
463	
464	.. index:: ! data count section, data count, data segment
465	   pair: binary format; data count
466	   pair: section; data count
467	.. _binary-datacountsec:
468	
469	Data Count Section
470	~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
471	
472	The *data count section* has the id 12.
473	It decodes into an optional :ref:`u32 <syntax-uint>` that represents the number of :ref:`data segments <syntax-data>` in the :ref:`data section <binary-datasec>`. If this count does not match the length of the data segment vector, the module is malformed.
474	
475	.. math::
476	   \begin{array}{llclll}
477	   \production{data count section} & \Bdatacountsec &::=&
478	     \X{n}^?{:}\Bsection_{12}(\Bu32) &\Rightarrow& \X{n}^? \\
479	   \end{array}
480	
481	.. note::
482	   The data count section is used to simplify single-pass validation. Since the
483	   data section occurs after the code section, the :math:`\MEMORYINIT` and
484	   :math:`\DATADROP` instructions would not be able to check whether the data
485	   segment index is valid until the data section is read. The data count section
486	   occurs before the code section, so a single-pass validator can use this count
487	   instead of deferring validation.
488

490	.. index:: module, section, type definition, function type, function, table, memory, global, element, data, start function, import, export, context, version
491	   pair: binary format; module
492	.. _binary-magic:
493	.. _binary-version:
494	.. _binary-module:
495	
496	Modules
497	~~~~~~~
498	
499	The encoding of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>` starts with a preamble containing a 4-byte magic number (the string :math:`\text{\backslash0asm}`) and a version field.
500	The current version of the WebAssembly binary format is 1.
501	
502	The preamble is followed by a sequence of :ref:`sections <binary-section>`.
503	:ref:`Custom sections <binary-customsec>` may be inserted at any place in this sequence,
504	while other sections must occur at most once and in the prescribed order.
505	All sections can be empty.
506	
507	The lengths of vectors produced by the (possibly empty) :ref:`function <binary-funcsec>` and :ref:`code <binary-codesec>` section must match up.
508	
509	Similarly, the optional data count must match the length of the :ref:`data segment <binary-datasec>` vector.
510	Furthermore, it must be present if any :ref:`data index <syntax-dataidx>` occurs in the code section.
511	
512	.. math::
513	   \begin{array}{llcllll}
514	   \production{magic} & \Bmagic &::=&
515	     \hex{00}~\hex{61}~\hex{73}~\hex{6D} \\
516	   \production{version} & \Bversion &::=&
517	     \hex{01}~\hex{00}~\hex{00}~\hex{00} \\
518	   \production{module} & \Bmodule &::=&
519	     \Bmagic \\ &&&
520	     \Bversion \\ &&&
521	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
522	     \functype^\ast{:\,}\Btypesec \\ &&&
523	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
524	     \import^\ast{:\,}\Bimportsec \\ &&&
525	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
526	     \typeidx^n{:\,}\Bfuncsec \\ &&&
527	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
528	     \table^\ast{:\,}\Btablesec \\ &&&
529	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
530	     \mem^\ast{:\,}\Bmemsec \\ &&&
531	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
532	     \global^\ast{:\,}\Bglobalsec \\ &&&
533	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
534	     \export^\ast{:\,}\Bexportsec \\ &&&
535	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
536	     \start^?{:\,}\Bstartsec \\ &&&
537	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
538	     \elem^\ast{:\,}\Belemsec \\ &&&
539	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
540	     m^?{:\,}\Bdatacountsec \\ &&&
541	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
542	     \X{code}^n{:\,}\Bcodesec \\ &&&
543	     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
544	     \data^m{:\,}\Bdatasec \\ &&&
545	     \Bcustomsec^\ast
546	     \quad\Rightarrow\quad \{~
547	       \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
548	       \MTYPES~\functype^\ast, \\
549	       \MFUNCS~\func^n, \\
550	       \MTABLES~\table^\ast, \\
551	       \MMEMS~\mem^\ast, \\
552	       \MGLOBALS~\global^\ast, \\
553	       \MELEMS~\elem^\ast, \\
554	       \MDATAS~\data^m, \\
555	       \MSTART~\start^?, \\
556	       \MIMPORTS~\import^\ast, \\
557	       \MEXPORTS~\export^\ast ~\} \\
558	       \end{array} \\ &&&
559	     (\iff m^? \neq \epsilon \vee \freedataidx(\X{code}^n) = \emptyset) \\
560	   \end{array}
561	
562	where for each :math:`t_i^\ast, e_i` in :math:`\X{code}^n`,
563	
564	.. math::
565	   \func^n[i] = \{ \FTYPE~\typeidx^n[i], \FLOCALS~t_i^\ast, \FBODY~e_i \} \\
566	
567	.. note::
568	   The version of the WebAssembly binary format may increase in the future
569	   if backward-incompatible changes have to be made to the format.
570	   However, such changes are expected to occur very infrequently, if ever.
571	   The binary format is intended to be extensible,
572	   such that future features can be added without incrementing its version.
573

file.content:
Modules
-------

The binary encoding of modules is organized into *sections*.
Most sections correspond to one component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>` record,
except that :ref:`function definitions <syntax-func>` are split into two sections, separating their type declarations in the :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>` from their bodies in the :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`.

.. note::
   This separation enables *parallel* and *streaming* compilation of the functions in a module.


.. index:: index, type index, function index, table index, memory index, global index, element index, data index, local index, label index
   pair: binary format; type index

   pair: binary format; global index

.. _binary-typeidx:
.. _binary-funcidx:

.. _binary-index:

Indices
~~~~~~~

All :ref:`indices <syntax-index>` are encoded with their respective value.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{type index} & \Btypeidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{function index} & \Bfuncidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{table index} & \Btableidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{memory index} & \Bmemidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{global index} & \Bglobalidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{element index} & \Belemidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{data index} & \Bdataidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{local index} & \Blocalidx &::=& x{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& x \\
   \production{label index} & \Blabelidx &::=& l{:}\Bu32 &\Rightarrow& l \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! section
   pair: binary format; section
.. _binary-section:

Sections
~~~~~~~~

Each section consists of

* a one-byte section *id*,
* the |U32| *size* of the contents, in bytes,
* the actual *contents*, whose structure is dependent on the section id.

Every section is optional; an omitted section is equivalent to the section being present with empty contents.

The following parameterized grammar rule defines the generic structure of a section with id :math:`N` and contents described by the grammar :math:`\B{B}`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad}l}
   \production{section} & \Bsection_N(\B{B}) &::=&
     N{:}\Bbyte~~\X{size}{:}\Bu32~~\X{cont}{:}\B{B}
       &\Rightarrow& \X{cont} & (\iff \X{size} = ||\B{B}||) \\ &&|&
     \epsilon &\Rightarrow& \epsilon
   \end{array}

For most sections, the contents :math:`\B{B}` encodes a :ref:`vector <binary-vec>`.
In these cases, the empty result :math:`\epsilon` is interpreted as the empty vector.

.. note::
   Other than for unknown :ref:`custom sections <binary-customsec>`,
   the :math:`\X{size}` is not required for decoding, but can be used to skip sections when navigating through a binary.
   The module is malformed if the size does not match the length of the binary contents :math:`\B{B}`.

The following section ids are used:

==  ===============================================
Id  Section                                        
==  ===============================================
 0  :ref:`custom section <binary-customsec>`       
 1  :ref:`type section <binary-typesec>`           
 2  :ref:`import section <binary-importsec>`       
 3  :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>`       
 4  :ref:`table section <binary-tablesec>`         
 5  :ref:`memory section <binary-memsec>`          
 6  :ref:`global section <binary-globalsec>`       
 7  :ref:`export section <binary-exportsec>`       
 8  :ref:`start section <binary-startsec>`         
 9  :ref:`element section <binary-elemsec>`        
10  :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`           
11  :ref:`data section <binary-datasec>`           
12  :ref:`data count section <binary-datacountsec>`
==  ===============================================

.. note::
   Section ids do not always correspond to the :ref:`order of sections <binary-module>` in the encoding of a module.


.. index:: ! custom section
   pair: binary format; custom section
   single: section; custom
.. _binary-customsec:

Custom Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

*Custom sections* have the id 0.
They are intended to be used for debugging information or third-party extensions, and are ignored by the WebAssembly semantics.
Their contents consist of a :ref:`name <syntax-name>` further identifying the custom section, followed by an uninterpreted sequence of bytes for custom use.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{custom section} & \Bcustomsec &::=&
     \Bsection_0(\Bcustom) \\
   \production{custom data} & \Bcustom &::=&
     \Bname~~\Bbyte^\ast \\
   \end{array}

.. note::
   If an implementation interprets the data of a custom section, then errors in that data, or the placement of the section, must not invalidate the module.


.. index:: ! type section, type definition
   pair: binary format; type section
   pair: section; type
.. _binary-typedef:
.. _binary-typesec:

Type Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *type section* has the id 1.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`function types <syntax-functype>` that represent the |MTYPES| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{type section} & \Btypesec &::=&
     \X{ft}^\ast{:\,}\Bsection_1(\Bvec(\Bfunctype)) &\Rightarrow& \X{ft}^\ast \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! import section, import, name, function type, table type, memory type, global type
   pair: binary format; import
   pair: section; import
.. _binary-import:
.. _binary-importdesc:
.. _binary-importsec:

Import Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *import section* has the id 2.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`imports <syntax-import>` that represent the |MIMPORTS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{import section} & \Bimportsec &::=&
     \X{im}^\ast{:}\Bsection_2(\Bvec(\Bimport)) &\Rightarrow& \X{im}^\ast \\
   \production{import} & \Bimport &::=&
     \X{mod}{:}\Bname~~\X{nm}{:}\Bname~~d{:}\Bimportdesc
       &\Rightarrow& \{ \IMODULE~\X{mod}, \INAME~\X{nm}, \IDESC~d \} \\
   \production{import description} & \Bimportdesc &::=&
     \hex{00}~~x{:}\Btypeidx &\Rightarrow& \IDFUNC~x \\ &&|&
     \hex{01}~~\X{tt}{:}\Btabletype &\Rightarrow& \IDTABLE~\X{tt} \\ &&|&
     \hex{02}~~\X{mt}{:}\Bmemtype &\Rightarrow& \IDMEM~\X{mt} \\ &&|&
     \hex{03}~~\X{gt}{:}\Bglobaltype &\Rightarrow& \IDGLOBAL~\X{gt} \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! function section, function, type index, function type
   pair: binary format; function
   pair: section; function
.. _binary-funcsec:

Function Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *function section* has the id 3.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`type indices <syntax-typeidx>` that represent the |FTYPE| fields of the :ref:`functions <syntax-func>` in the |MFUNCS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
The |FLOCALS| and |FBODY| fields of the respective functions are encoded separately in the :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{function section} & \Bfuncsec &::=&
     x^\ast{:}\Bsection_3(\Bvec(\Btypeidx)) &\Rightarrow& x^\ast \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! table section, table, table type
   pair: binary format; table
   pair: section; table
.. _binary-table:
.. _binary-tablesec:

Table Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *table section* has the id 4.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`tables <syntax-table>` that represent the |MTABLES| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{table section} & \Btablesec &::=&
     \X{tab}^\ast{:}\Bsection_4(\Bvec(\Btable)) &\Rightarrow& \X{tab}^\ast \\
   \production{table} & \Btable &::=&
     \X{tt}{:}\Btabletype &\Rightarrow& \{ \TTYPE~\X{tt} \} \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! memory section, memory, memory type
   pair: binary format; memory
   pair: section; memory
.. _binary-mem:
.. _binary-memsec:

Memory Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *memory section* has the id 5.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`memories <syntax-mem>` that represent the |MMEMS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{memory section} & \Bmemsec &::=&
     \X{mem}^\ast{:}\Bsection_5(\Bvec(\Bmem)) &\Rightarrow& \X{mem}^\ast \\
   \production{memory} & \Bmem &::=&
     \X{mt}{:}\Bmemtype &\Rightarrow& \{ \MTYPE~\X{mt} \} \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! global section, global, global type, expression
   pair: binary format; global
   pair: section; global
.. _binary-global:
.. _binary-globalsec:

Global Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *global section* has the id 6.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`globals <syntax-global>` that represent the |MGLOBALS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{global section} & \Bglobalsec &::=&
     \X{glob}^\ast{:}\Bsection_6(\Bvec(\Bglobal)) &\Rightarrow& \X{glob}^\ast \\
   \production{global} & \Bglobal &::=&
     \X{gt}{:}\Bglobaltype~~e{:}\Bexpr
       &\Rightarrow& \{ \GTYPE~\X{gt}, \GINIT~e \} \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! export section, export, name, index, function index, table index, memory index, global index
   pair: binary format; export
   pair: section; export
.. _binary-export:
.. _binary-exportdesc:
.. _binary-exportsec:

Export Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *export section* has the id 7.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`exports <syntax-export>` that represent the |MEXPORTS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{export section} & \Bexportsec &::=&
     \X{ex}^\ast{:}\Bsection_7(\Bvec(\Bexport)) &\Rightarrow& \X{ex}^\ast \\
   \production{export} & \Bexport &::=&
     \X{nm}{:}\Bname~~d{:}\Bexportdesc
       &\Rightarrow& \{ \ENAME~\X{nm}, \EDESC~d \} \\
   \production{export description} & \Bexportdesc &::=&
     \hex{00}~~x{:}\Bfuncidx &\Rightarrow& \EDFUNC~x \\ &&|&
     \hex{01}~~x{:}\Btableidx &\Rightarrow& \EDTABLE~x \\ &&|&
     \hex{02}~~x{:}\Bmemidx &\Rightarrow& \EDMEM~x \\ &&|&
     \hex{03}~~x{:}\Bglobalidx &\Rightarrow& \EDGLOBAL~x \\
   \end{array}

Start Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *start section* has the id 8.
It decodes into an optional :ref:`start function <syntax-start>` that represents the |MSTART| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{start section} & \Bstartsec &::=&
     \X{st}^?{:}\Bsection_8(\Bstart) &\Rightarrow& \X{st}^? \\
   \production{start function} & \Bstart &::=&
     x{:}\Bfuncidx &\Rightarrow& \{ \SFUNC~x \} \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: ! element section, element, table index, expression, function index
   pair: binary format; element
   pair: section; element
   single: table; element
   single: element; segment
.. _binary-elem:
.. _binary-elemsec:
.. _binary-elemkind:

Element Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *element section* has the id 9.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`element segments <syntax-elem>` that represent the |MELEMS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{element section} & \Belemsec &::=&
     \X{seg}^\ast{:}\Bsection_9(\Bvec(\Belem)) &\Rightarrow& \X{seg}^\ast \\
   \production{element segment} & \Belem &::=&
     0{:}\Bu32~~e{:}\Bexpr~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~\FUNCREF, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~0, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
     1{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Belemkind~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~\X{et}, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EPASSIVE \} \\ &&|&
     2{:}\Bu32~~x{:}\Btableidx~~e{:}\Bexpr~~\X{et}:\Belemkind~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~\X{et}, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~x, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
     3{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Belemkind~~y^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bfuncidx)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~\X{et}, \EINIT~((\REFFUNC~y)~\END)^\ast, \EMODE~\EDECLARATIVE \} \\ &&|&
     4{:}\Bu32~~e{:}\Bexpr~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~\FUNCREF, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~0, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
     5{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Breftype~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~et, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EPASSIVE \} \\ &&|&
     6{:}\Bu32~~x{:}\Btableidx~~e{:}\Bexpr~~\X{et}:\Breftype~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~et, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EACTIVE~\{ \ETABLE~x, \EOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
     7{:}\Bu32~~\X{et}:\Breftype~~\X{el}^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bexpr)
       &\Rightarrow& \\&&&\quad
       \{ \ETYPE~et, \EINIT~\X{el}^\ast, \EMODE~\EDECLARATIVE \} \\
   \production{element kind} & \Belemkind &::=&
     \hex{00} &\Rightarrow& \FUNCREF \\
   \end{array}

.. note::
   The initial integer can be interpreted as a bitfield.
   Bit 0 distinguishes a passive or declarative segment from an active segment,
   bit 1 indicates the presence of an explicit table index for an active segment and otherwise distinguishes passive from declarative segments,
   bit 2 indicates the use of element type and element :ref:`expressions <binary-expr>` instead of element kind and element indices.

   Additional element kinds may be added in future versions of WebAssembly.


.. index:: ! code section, function, local, type index, function type
   pair: binary format; function
   pair: binary format; local
   pair: section; code
.. _binary-code:
.. _binary-func:
.. _binary-local:
.. _binary-codesec:

Code Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *code section* has the id 10.
It decodes into a vector of *code* entries that are pairs of :ref:`value type <syntax-valtype>` vectors and :ref:`expressions <syntax-expr>`.
They represent the |FLOCALS| and |FBODY| field of the :ref:`functions <syntax-func>` in the |MFUNCS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.
The |FTYPE| fields of the respective functions are encoded separately in the :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>`.

The encoding of each code entry consists of

* the |U32| *size* of the function code in bytes,
* the actual *function code*, which in turn consists of

  * the declaration of *locals*,
  * the function *body* as an :ref:`expression <binary-expr>`.

Local declarations are compressed into a vector whose entries consist of

* a |U32| *count*,
* a :ref:`value type <binary-valtype>`,

denoting *count* locals of the same value type.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad}l}
   \production{code section} & \Bcodesec &::=&
     \X{code}^\ast{:}\Bsection_{10}(\Bvec(\Bcode))
       &\Rightarrow& \X{code}^\ast \\
   \production{code} & \Bcode &::=&
     \X{size}{:}\Bu32~~\X{code}{:}\Bfunc
       &\Rightarrow& \X{code} & (\iff \X{size} = ||\Bfunc||) \\
   \production{function} & \Bfunc &::=&
     (t^\ast)^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Blocals)~~e{:}\Bexpr
       &\Rightarrow& \concat((t^\ast)^\ast), e
         & (\iff |\concat((t^\ast)^\ast)| < 2^{32}) \\
   \production{locals} & \Blocals &::=&
     n{:}\Bu32~~t{:}\Bvaltype &\Rightarrow& t^n \\
   \end{array}

Here, :math:`\X{code}` ranges over pairs :math:`(\valtype^\ast, \expr)`.
The meta function :math:`\concat((t^\ast)^\ast)` concatenates all sequences :math:`t_i^\ast` in :math:`(t^\ast)^\ast`.
Any code for which the length of the resulting sequence is out of bounds of the maximum size of a :ref:`vector <syntax-vec>` is malformed.

.. note::
   Like with :ref:`sections <binary-section>`, the code :math:`\X{size}` is not needed for decoding, but can be used to skip functions when navigating through a binary.
   The module is malformed if a size does not match the length of the respective function code.


.. index:: ! data section, data, memory, memory index, expression, byte
   pair: binary format; data
   pair: section; data
   single: memory; data
   single: data; segment
.. _binary-data:
.. _binary-datasec:

Data Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *data section* has the id 11.
It decodes into a vector of :ref:`data segments <syntax-data>` that represent the |MDATAS| component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{data section} & \Bdatasec &::=&
     \X{seg}^\ast{:}\Bsection_{11}(\Bvec(\Bdata)) &\Rightarrow& \X{seg}^\ast \\
   \production{data segment} & \Bdata &::=&
     0{:}\Bu32~~e{:}\Bexpr~~b^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bbyte)
       &\Rightarrow& \{ \DINIT~b^\ast, \DMODE~\DACTIVE~\{ \DMEM~0, \DOFFSET~e \} \} \\ &&|&
     1{:}\Bu32~~b^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bbyte)
       &\Rightarrow& \{ \DINIT~b^\ast, \DMODE~\DPASSIVE \} \\ &&|&
     2{:}\Bu32~~x{:}\Bmemidx~~e{:}\Bexpr~~b^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bbyte)
       &\Rightarrow& \{ \DINIT~b^\ast, \DMODE~\DACTIVE~\{ \DMEM~x, \DOFFSET~e \} \} \\
   \end{array}

.. note::
   The initial integer can be interpreted as a bitfield.
   Bit 0 indicates a passive segment,
   bit 1 indicates the presence of an explicit memory index for an active segment.

   In the current version of WebAssembly, at most one memory may be defined or
   imported in a single module, so all valid :ref:`active <syntax-data>` data
   segments have a |DMEM| value of :math:`0`.


.. index:: ! data count section, data count, data segment
   pair: binary format; data count
   pair: section; data count
.. _binary-datacountsec:

Data Count Section
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The *data count section* has the id 12.
It decodes into an optional :ref:`u32 <syntax-uint>` that represents the number of :ref:`data segments <syntax-data>` in the :ref:`data section <binary-datasec>`. If this count does not match the length of the data segment vector, the module is malformed.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{data count section} & \Bdatacountsec &::=&
     \X{n}^?{:}\Bsection_{12}(\Bu32) &\Rightarrow& \X{n}^? \\
   \end{array}

.. note::
   The data count section is used to simplify single-pass validation. Since the
   data section occurs after the code section, the :math:`\MEMORYINIT` and
   :math:`\DATADROP` instructions would not be able to check whether the data
   segment index is valid until the data section is read. The data count section
   occurs before the code section, so a single-pass validator can use this count
   instead of deferring validation.


.. index:: module, section, type definition, function type, function, table, memory, global, element, data, start function, import, export, context, version
   pair: binary format; module
.. _binary-magic:
.. _binary-version:
.. _binary-module:

Modules
~~~~~~~

The encoding of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>` starts with a preamble containing a 4-byte magic number (the string :math:`\text{\backslash0asm}`) and a version field.
The current version of the WebAssembly binary format is 1.

The preamble is followed by a sequence of :ref:`sections <binary-section>`.
:ref:`Custom sections <binary-customsec>` may be inserted at any place in this sequence,
while other sections must occur at most once and in the prescribed order.
All sections can be empty.

The lengths of vectors produced by the (possibly empty) :ref:`function <binary-funcsec>` and :ref:`code <binary-codesec>` section must match up.

Similarly, the optional data count must match the length of the :ref:`data segment <binary-datasec>` vector.
Furthermore, it must be present if any :ref:`data index <syntax-dataidx>` occurs in the code section.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llcllll}
   \production{magic} & \Bmagic &::=&
     \hex{00}~\hex{61}~\hex{73}~\hex{6D} \\
   \production{version} & \Bversion &::=&
     \hex{01}~\hex{00}~\hex{00}~\hex{00} \\
   \production{module} & \Bmodule &::=&
     \Bmagic \\ &&&
     \Bversion \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \functype^\ast{:\,}\Btypesec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \import^\ast{:\,}\Bimportsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \typeidx^n{:\,}\Bfuncsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \table^\ast{:\,}\Btablesec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \mem^\ast{:\,}\Bmemsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \global^\ast{:\,}\Bglobalsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \export^\ast{:\,}\Bexportsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \start^?{:\,}\Bstartsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \elem^\ast{:\,}\Belemsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     m^?{:\,}\Bdatacountsec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \X{code}^n{:\,}\Bcodesec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast \\ &&&
     \data^m{:\,}\Bdatasec \\ &&&
     \Bcustomsec^\ast
     \quad\Rightarrow\quad \{~
       \begin{array}[t]{@{}l@{}}
       \MTYPES~\functype^\ast, \\
       \MFUNCS~\func^n, \\
       \MTABLES~\table^\ast, \\
       \MMEMS~\mem^\ast, \\
       \MGLOBALS~\global^\ast, \\
       \MELEMS~\elem^\ast, \\
       \MDATAS~\data^m, \\
       \MSTART~\start^?, \\
       \MIMPORTS~\import^\ast, \\
       \MEXPORTS~\export^\ast ~\} \\
       \end{array} \\ &&&
     (\iff m^? \neq \epsilon \vee \freedataidx(\X{code}^n) = \emptyset) \\
   \end{array}

where for each :math:`t_i^\ast, e_i` in :math:`\X{code}^n`,

.. math::
   \func^n[i] = \{ \FTYPE~\typeidx^n[i], \FLOCALS~t_i^\ast, \FBODY~e_i \} \\

.. note::
   The version of the WebAssembly binary format may increase in the future
   if backward-incompatible changes have to be made to the format.
   However, such changes are expected to occur very infrequently, if ever.
   The binary format is intended to be extensible,
   such that future features can be added without incrementing its version.

Number Types
~~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Number types <syntax-numtype>` are encoded by a single byte.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad\qquad}l}
   \production{number type} & \Bnumtype &::=&
     \hex{7F} &\Rightarrow& \I32 \\ &&|&
     \hex{7E} &\Rightarrow& \I64 \\ &&|&
     \hex{7D} &\Rightarrow& \F32 \\ &&|&
     \hex{7C} &\Rightarrow& \F64 \\
   \end{array}

Vector Types
~~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Vector types <syntax-vectype>` are also encoded by a single byte.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad\qquad}l}
   \production{vector type} & \Bvectype &::=&
     \hex{7B} &\Rightarrow& \V128 \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: reference type

Reference Types
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Reference types <syntax-reftype>` are also encoded by a single byte.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad\qquad}l}
   \production{reference type} & \Breftype &::=&

~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Value types <syntax-valtype>` are encoded with their respective encoding as a :ref:`number type <binary-numtype>`, :ref:`vector type <binary-vectype>`, or :ref:`reference type <binary-reftype>`.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll@{\qquad\qquad}l}
   \production{value type} & \Bvaltype &::=&
     t{:}\Bnumtype &\Rightarrow& t \\ &&|&
     t{:}\Bvectype &\Rightarrow& t \\ &&|&
     t{:}\Breftype &\Rightarrow& t \\
   \end{array}

.. note::
   Value types can occur in contexts where :ref:`type indices <syntax-typeidx>` are also allowed, such as in the case of :ref:`block types <binary-blocktype>`.
   Thus, the binary format for types corresponds to the |SignedLEB128|_ :ref:`encoding <binary-sint>` of small negative :math:`\sN` values, so that they can coexist with (positive) type indices in the future.

~~~~~~~~~~~~

.. math::

     t^\ast{:\,}\Bvec(\Bvaltype) &\Rightarrow& [t^\ast] \\
   \end{array}

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

   \production{function type} & \Bfunctype &::=&
     \hex{60}~~\X{rt}_1{:\,}\Bresulttype~~\X{rt}_2{:\,}\Bresulttype
       &\Rightarrow& \X{rt}_1 \to \X{rt}_2 \\
   \end{array}


.. index:: limits
   pair: binary format; limits
.. _binary-limits:

Limits
~~~~~~

:ref:`Limits <syntax-limits>` are encoded with a preceding flag indicating whether a maximum is present.

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{limits} & \Blimits &::=&

~~~~~~~~~~~~

Global Types
~~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Global types <syntax-globaltype>` are encoded by their :ref:`value type <binary-valtype>` and a flag for their :ref:`mutability <syntax-mut>`.

     \hex{00} &\Rightarrow& \MCONST \\ &&|&
     \hex{01} &\Rightarrow& \MVAR \\
   \end{array}

.. index:: instruction, ! opcode
.. _binary-instr:

Instructions
------------

:ref:`Instructions <syntax-instr>` are encoded by *opcodes*.
Each opcode is represented by a single byte,
and is followed by the instruction's immediate arguments, where present.
The only exception are :ref:`structured control instructions <binary-instr-control>`, which consist of several opcodes bracketing their nested instruction sequences.

.. note::
   Gaps in the byte code ranges for encoding instructions are reserved for future extensions.


.. index:: control instructions, structured control, label, block, branch, result type, value type, block type, label index, function index, type index, vector, polymorphism, LEB128
   pair: binary format; instruction
   pair: binary format; block type
.. _binary-instr-control:

Control Instructions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Control instructions <syntax-instr-control>` have varying encodings. For structured instructions, the instruction sequences forming nested blocks are terminated with explicit opcodes for |END| and |ELSE|.

:ref:`Block types <syntax-blocktype>` are encoded in special compressed form, by either the byte :math:`\hex{40}` indicating the empty type, as a single :ref:`value type <binary-valtype>`, or as a :ref:`type index <binary-typeidx>` encoded as a positive :ref:`signed integer <binary-sint>`.

.. _binary-blocktype:
.. _binary-nop:
.. _binary-unreachable:
.. _binary-block:
.. _binary-loop:
.. _binary-if:
.. _binary-br:
.. _binary-br_if:
.. _binary-br_table:
.. _binary-return:
.. _binary-call:
.. _binary-call_indirect:

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llcllll}
   \production{block type} & \Bblocktype &::=&
     \hex{40} &\Rightarrow& \epsilon \\ &&|&
     t{:}\Bvaltype &\Rightarrow& t \\ &&|&
     x{:}\Bs33 &\Rightarrow& x & (\iff x \geq 0) \\
   \production{instruction} & \Binstr &::=&
     \hex{00} &\Rightarrow& \UNREACHABLE \\ &&|&
     \hex{01} &\Rightarrow& \NOP \\ &&|&
     \hex{02}~~\X{bt}{:}\Bblocktype~~(\X{in}{:}\Binstr)^\ast~~\hex{0B}
       &\Rightarrow& \BLOCK~\X{bt}~\X{in}^\ast~\END \\ &&|&
     \hex{03}~~\X{bt}{:}\Bblocktype~~(\X{in}{:}\Binstr)^\ast~~\hex{0B}
       &\Rightarrow& \LOOP~\X{bt}~\X{in}^\ast~\END \\ &&|&
     \hex{04}~~\X{bt}{:}\Bblocktype~~(\X{in}{:}\Binstr)^\ast~~\hex{0B}
       &\Rightarrow& \IF~\X{bt}~\X{in}^\ast~\ELSE~\epsilon~\END \\ &&|&
     \hex{04}~~\X{bt}{:}\Bblocktype~~(\X{in}_1{:}\Binstr)^\ast~~
       \hex{05}~~(\X{in}_2{:}\Binstr)^\ast~~\hex{0B}
       &\Rightarrow& \IF~\X{bt}~\X{in}_1^\ast~\ELSE~\X{in}_2^\ast~\END \\ &&|&
     \hex{0C}~~l{:}\Blabelidx &\Rightarrow& \BR~l \\ &&|&
     \hex{0D}~~l{:}\Blabelidx &\Rightarrow& \BRIF~l \\ &&|&
     \hex{0E}~~l^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Blabelidx)~~l_N{:}\Blabelidx
       &\Rightarrow& \BRTABLE~l^\ast~l_N \\ &&|&
     \hex{0F} &\Rightarrow& \RETURN \\ &&|&
     \hex{10}~~x{:}\Bfuncidx &\Rightarrow& \CALL~x \\ &&|&
     \hex{11}~~y{:}\Btypeidx~~x{:}\Btableidx &\Rightarrow& \CALLINDIRECT~x~y \\ &&|&
     \dots
   \end{array}

.. note::
   The |ELSE| opcode :math:`\hex{05}` in the encoding of an |IF| instruction can be omitted if the following instruction sequence is empty.

   Unlike any :ref:`other occurrence <binary-typeidx>`, the :ref:`type index <syntax-typeidx>` in a :ref:`block type <syntax-blocktype>` is encoded as a positive :ref:`signed integer <syntax-sint>`, so that its |SignedLEB128| bit pattern cannot collide with the encoding of :ref:`value types <binary-valtype>` or the special code :math:`\hex{40}`, which correspond to the LEB128 encoding of negative integers.
   To avoid any loss in the range of allowed indices, it is treated as a 33 bit signed integer.


.. index:: reference instruction
   pair: binary format; instruction
.. _binary-instr-ref:

Reference Instructions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

:ref:`Reference instructions <syntax-instr-ref>` are represented by single byte codes.

.. _binary-ref.null:
.. _binary-ref.func:

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{instruction} & \Binstr &::=& \dots \\ &&|&
     \hex{D0}~~t{:}\Breftype &\Rightarrow& \REFNULL~t \\ &&|&
     \hex{D1} &\Rightarrow& \REFISNULL \\ &&|&
     \hex{D2}~~x{:}\Bfuncidx &\Rightarrow& \REFFUNC~x \\
   \end{array}

   pair: binary format; instruction

:ref:`Parametric instructions <syntax-instr-parametric>` are represented by single byte codes, possibly followed by a type annotation.

     \hex{1A} &\Rightarrow& \DROP \\ &&|&
     \hex{1B} &\Rightarrow& \SELECT \\ &&|&
     \hex{1C}~~t^\ast{:}\Bvec(\Bvaltype) &\Rightarrow& \SELECT~t^\ast \\
   \end{array}

.. _binary-instr-numeric:

Numeric Instructions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

All variants of :ref:`numeric instructions <syntax-instr-numeric>` are represented by separate byte codes.

The |CONST| instructions are followed by the respective literal.

.. _binary-const:

.. math::
   \begin{array}{llclll}
   \production{instruction} & \Binstr &::=& \dots \\&&|&
     \hex{41}~~n{:}\Bi32 &\Rightarrow& \I32.\CONST~n \\ &&|&
     \hex{42}~~n{:}\Bi64 &\Rightarrow& \I64.\CONST~n \\ &&|&
     \hex{43}~~z{:}\Bf32 &\Rightarrow& \F32.\CONST~z \\ &&|&
     \hex{44}~~z{:}\Bf64 &\Rightarrow& \F64.\CONST~z \\
   \end{array}

All other numeric instructions are plain opcodes without any immediates.

1	Modules
2	-------
3	
4	The binary encoding of modules is organized into *sections*.
5	Most sections correspond to one component of a :ref:`module <syntax-module>` record,
6	except that :ref:`function definitions <syntax-func>` are split into two sections, separating their type declarations in the :ref:`function section <binary-funcsec>` from their bodies in the :ref:`code section <binary-codesec>`.
7	
8	.. note::
9	   This separation enables *parallel* and *streaming* compilation of the functions in a module.
